answers.explanation: Sender and receiver both know G, because it's part of the standard.
G is r + 1 bits, so r = 3.
No carries, no borrows: 1 + 1 = 0 and 1 - 1 = 0, the same as XOR.
Then the receiver can check by dividing: a zero remainder means no error was detected.
Any non-zero remainder means the bits changed in transit.
1101000 divided by 1011 (mod 2) leaves 001, so the sender transmits 1101001.
Append two zeros, 11010100, and divide by 101: the remainder is 11.
With G = 11 the CRC is a parity bit: 1011 has three 1s, so R = 1, making the count even.
A CRC with r bits detects all burst errors shorter than r + 1 bits.
Both carry a CRC-32 in their Frame Check Sequence.
That's why the NIC can check every frame at full line speed.
